Our Loan-Granting Self-Representations Corpus 2025 consists of a large corpus of 30 000 synthetic natural language self-descriptions derived from corresponding representations of applicants in the German Credit Dataset, along with expert annotations of representation mismatches between each pair of representations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Representation Fidelity as a new dimension for validating algorithmic decisions about humans by measuring whether decisions rest on reasonable grounds, operationalized through distance between externally prescribed input representations and human self-descriptions.
AI.motivation: Current algorithmic decision-making systems lack methods to validate whether decisions about individuals are based on reasonable grounds. There's a need to measure the fidelity of representations used in these systems to ensure they accurately reflect the human subjects they represent.
AI.method: Proposes measuring distance between two representations: (1) externally prescribed input representation used for decision-making, and (2) self-description provided by the human subject. Develops methods to quantify discrepancies, derives a typology of representation mismatches, and creates a benchmark dataset for evaluation.
AI.result: Introduces the Loan-Granting Self-Representations Corpus 2025 with 30,000 synthetic natural language self-descriptions derived from the German Credit Dataset, along with expert annotations of representation mismatches between each pair of representations.
AI.conclusion: Representation Fidelity provides a novel validation dimension for algorithmic decisions, enabling assessment of whether decisions rest on reasonable grounds through systematic comparison of external and self-representations, with practical applications demonstrated in loan-granting contexts.

title: UniSTOK: Uniform Inductive Spatio-Temporal Kriging
summary: Spatio-temporal kriging aims to infer signals at unobserved locations from observed sensors and is critical to applications such as transportation and environmental monitoring. In practice, however, observed sensors themselves often exhibit heterogeneous missingness, forcing inductive kriging models to rely on crudely imputed inputs. This setting brings three key challenges: (1) it is unclear whether an value is a true signal or a missingness-induced artifact; (2) missingness is highly heterogeneous across sensors and time; (3) missing observations distort the local spatio-temporal structure. To address these issues, we propose Uniform Inductive Spatio-Temporal Kriging (UniSTOK), a plug-and-play framework that enhances existing inductive kriging backbones under missing observation. Our framework forms a dual-branch input consisting of the original observations and a jigsaw-augmented counterpart that synthesizes proxy signals only at missing entries. The two branches are then processed in parallel by a shared spatio-temporal backbone with explicit missingness mask modulation. Their outputs are finally adaptively fused via dual-channel attention. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets under diverse missing patterns demonstrate consistent and significant improvements.

AI.tldr: UniSTOK is a plug-and-play framework that enhances inductive spatio-temporal kriging models by handling heterogeneous missing data through dual-branch processing with jigsaw augmentation and missingness mask modulation.
AI.motivation: Real-world spatio-temporal kriging faces challenges with heterogeneous missing data in sensor observations, where missing values create artifacts, vary across sensors/time, and distort local spatio-temporal structures, making traditional approaches unreliable.
AI.method: Proposes UniSTOK with dual-branch input: original observations and jigsaw-augmented counterpart generating proxy signals at missing entries. Uses shared spatio-temporal backbone with explicit missingness mask modulation and adaptive fusion via dual-channel attention.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple real-world datasets under diverse missing patterns show consistent and significant improvements over existing inductive kriging methods.
AI.conclusion: UniSTOK effectively addresses heterogeneous missingness in spatio-temporal kriging through its dual-branch architecture with jigsaw augmentation and mask modulation, providing a robust plug-and-play solution for real-world applications.

title: Feature Resemblance: On the Theoretical Understanding of Analogical Reasoning in Transformers
summary: Understanding reasoning in large language models is complicated by evaluations that conflate multiple reasoning types. We isolate analogical reasoning (inferring shared properties between entities based on known similarities) and analyze its emergence in transformers. We theoretically prove three key results: (1) Joint training on similarity and attribution premises enables analogical reasoning through aligned representations; (2) Sequential training succeeds only when similarity structure is learned before specific attributes, revealing a necessary curriculum; (3) Two-hop reasoning ($a \to b, b \to c \implies a \to c$) reduces to analogical reasoning with identity bridges ($b = b$), which must appear explicitly in training data. These results reveal a unified mechanism: transformers encode entities with similar properties into similar representations, enabling property transfer through feature alignment. Experiments with architectures up to 1.5B parameters validate our theory and demonstrate how representational geometry shapes inductive reasoning capabilities.

AI.tldr: Transformers learn analogical reasoning through aligned representations when jointly trained on similarity and attribution premises, with specific curriculum requirements for sequential training.
AI.motivation: To isolate and understand analogical reasoning in transformers, separate from other reasoning types that are often conflated in evaluations, and to reveal the underlying mechanisms enabling this capability.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of transformer architectures with three key proofs: (1) joint training on similarity and attribution premises enables analogical reasoning through aligned representations, (2) sequential training requires specific curriculum order, (3) two-hop reasoning reduces to analogical reasoning with identity bridges. Experimental validation with architectures up to 1.5B parameters.
AI.result: Transformers encode entities with similar properties into similar representations, enabling property transfer through feature alignment. Joint training succeeds, while sequential training requires learning similarity structure before specific attributes. Two-hop reasoning emerges from analogical reasoning with explicit identity bridges in training data.
AI.conclusion: Analogical reasoning in transformers operates through a unified mechanism of representational alignment, where entities with similar properties are encoded into similar representations, enabling property transfer. The findings reveal specific curriculum requirements and training data conditions necessary for emergent reasoning capabilities.

title: Building AI Coding Agents for the Terminal: Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned
comment: Work in progress, new versions will be updated continuously
summary: The landscape of AI coding assistance is undergoing a fundamental shift from complex IDE plugins to versatile, terminal-native agents. Operating directly where developers manage source control, execute builds, and deploy environments, CLI-based agents offer unprecedented autonomy for long-horizon development tasks. In this paper, we present OPENDEV, an open-source, command-line coding agent engineered specifically for this new paradigm. Effective autonomous assistance requires strict safety controls and highly efficient context management to prevent context bloat and reasoning degradation. OPENDEV overcomes these challenges through a compound AI system architecture with workload-specialized model routing, a dual-agent architecture separating planning from execution, lazy tool discovery, and adaptive context compaction that progressively reduces older observations. Furthermore, it employs an automated memory system to accumulate project-specific knowledge across sessions and counteracts instruction fade-out through event-driven system reminders. By enforcing explicit reasoning phases and prioritizing context efficiency, OPENDEV provides a secure, extensible foundation for terminal-first AI assistance, offering a blueprint for robust autonomous software engineering.

AI.tldr: OPENDEV is an open-source CLI-based coding agent that operates directly in the terminal, offering autonomous assistance for long-horizon development tasks through a compound AI system architecture with specialized safety controls and context management.
AI.motivation: The AI coding assistance landscape is shifting from complex IDE plugins to terminal-native agents that operate where developers actually work (source control, builds, deployments). CLI-based agents offer unprecedented autonomy for long-horizon development tasks but require strict safety controls and efficient context management to prevent context bloat and reasoning degradation.
AI.method: OPENDEV employs a compound AI system architecture with: 1) Workload-specialized model routing, 2) Dual-agent architecture separating planning from execution, 3) Lazy tool discovery, 4) Adaptive context compaction that progressively reduces older observations, 5) Automated memory system for accumulating project-specific knowledge across sessions, and 6) Event-driven system reminders to counteract instruction fade-out.
AI.result: OPENDEV provides a secure, extensible foundation for terminal-first AI assistance by enforcing explicit reasoning phases and prioritizing context efficiency, offering a blueprint for robust autonomous software engineering.
AI.conclusion: OPENDEV represents a new paradigm in AI coding assistance - moving from IDE plugins to terminal-native agents - and demonstrates how compound AI system architectures with specialized safety controls and context management can enable effective autonomous assistance for long-horizon development tasks.

title: C2-Faith: Benchmarking LLM Judges for Causal and Coverage Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, but it remains unclear whether they can reliably assess process faithfulness rather than just answer plausibility. We introduce C2-Faith, a benchmark built from PRM800K that targets two complementary dimensions of faithfulness: causality (does each step logically follow from prior context?) and coverage (are essential intermediate inferences present?). Using controlled perturbations, we create examples with known causal error positions by replacing a single step with an acausal variant, and with controlled coverage deletions at varying deletion rates (scored against reference labels). We evaluate three frontier judges under three tasks: binary causal detection, causal step localization, and coverage scoring. The results show that model rankings depend strongly on task framing, with no single judge dominating all settings; all judges exhibit a substantial gap between detecting an error and localizing it; and coverage judgments are systematically inflated for incomplete reasoning. These findings clarify when LLM judges are dependable and where they fail, and provide practical guidance for selecting judges in process-level evaluation

AI.tldr: LLM judges struggle with reliably assessing faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning, showing task-dependent performance, difficulty localizing errors, and systematic inflation in coverage scoring.
AI.motivation: There's uncertainty about whether LLMs can reliably assess process faithfulness (causality and coverage) in chain-of-thought reasoning rather than just evaluating answer plausibility, necessitating systematic evaluation.
AI.method: Created C2-Faith benchmark from PRM800K with controlled perturbations: causal errors via single-step acausal replacements, and coverage errors via deletions at varying rates. Evaluated three frontier LLM judges on binary causal detection, causal step localization, and coverage scoring tasks.
AI.result: Model rankings depend strongly on task framing with no single judge dominating all settings; all judges show substantial gap between detecting errors and localizing them; coverage judgments are systematically inflated for incomplete reasoning.
AI.conclusion: LLM judges have limitations in process-level evaluation: their reliability varies by task, they struggle with error localization, and they overestimate coverage completeness, providing practical guidance for judge selection in faithfulness assessment.

title: Ailed: A Psyche-Driven Chess Engine with Dynamic Emotional Modulation
comment: 27 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables. Open source: https://github.com/chrnx-dev/ailed-chess
summary:
Chess engines passed human strength years ago, but they still don't play like humans. A grandmaster under clock pressure blunders in ways a club player on a hot streak never would. Conventional engines capture none of this.
  This paper proposes a personality x psyche decomposition to produce behavioral variability in chess play, drawing on patterns observed in human games. Personality is static -- a preset that pins down the engine's character. Psyche is dynamic -- a bounded scalar ψ_t \in [-100, +100], recomputed from five positional factors after every move. These two components feed into an audio-inspired signal chain (noise gate, compressor/expander, five-band equalizer, saturation limiter) that reshapes move probability distributions on the fly. The chain doesn't care what engine sits behind it: any system that outputs move probabilities will do. It needs no search and carries no state beyond ψ_t.
  I test the framework across 12,414 games against Maia2-1100, feeding it two probability sources that differ by ~2,800x in training data. Both show the same monotonic gradient in top-move agreement (~20-25 pp spread from stress to overconfidence), which tells us the behavioral variation comes from the signal chain, not from the model underneath. When the psyche runs overconfident, the chain mostly gets out of the way (66% agreement with vanilla Maia2). Under stress, the competitive score falls from 50.8% to 30.1%. The patterns are reminiscent of tilt and overconfidence as described in human play, but I should be upfront: this study includes no human-subject validation.

AI.tldr: A framework for introducing human-like behavioral variability in chess engines using personality (static) and psyche (dynamic) components that reshape move probabilities through an audio-inspired signal chain, creating patterns reminiscent of tilt and overconfidence without requiring human validation.
AI.motivation: Current chess engines lack human-like behavioral variability - they don't exhibit the psychological patterns seen in human play under pressure, such as blunders during time pressure or overconfidence during winning streaks. The paper aims to bridge this gap by creating engines that display more human-like psychological dynamics.
AI.method: Proposes a personality x psyche decomposition: personality is a static preset defining engine character, while psyche is a dynamic scalar ψ_t ∈ [-100,+100] recomputed after every move based on five positional factors. These feed into an audio-inspired signal chain (noise gate, compressor/expander, five-band equalizer, saturation limiter) that reshapes move probability distributions in real-time. The framework is engine-agnostic and requires no search or state beyond ψ_t.
AI.result: Tested across 12,414 games against Maia2-1100 using two probability sources differing by ~2,800x in training data. Both showed the same monotonic gradient in top-move agreement (~20-25 percentage point spread from stress to overconfidence), confirming behavioral variation comes from the signal chain. Under overconfidence: 66% agreement with vanilla Maia2. Under stress: competitive score dropped from 50.8% to 30.1%. Patterns resemble human tilt and overconfidence.
AI.conclusion: The personality x psyche framework successfully introduces human-like behavioral variability in chess engines through an audio-inspired signal chain that dynamically reshapes move probabilities. The approach is engine-agnostic and produces psychologically plausible patterns without requiring search or maintaining state. However, the study lacks human-subject validation to confirm the psychological realism of the generated behaviors.

title: Sparse-BitNet: 1.58-bit LLMs are Naturally Friendly to Semi-Structured Sparsity
summary: Semi-structured N:M sparsity and low-bit quantization (e.g., 1.58-bit BitNet) are two promising approaches for improving the efficiency of large language models (LLMs), yet they have largely been studied in isolation. In this work, we investigate their interaction and show that 1.58-bit BitNet is naturally more compatible with N:M sparsity than full-precision models. To study this effect, we propose Sparse-BitNet, a unified framework that jointly applies 1.58-bit quantization and dynamic N:M sparsification while ensuring stable training for the first time. Across multiple model scales and training regimes (sparse pretraining and dense-to-sparse schedules), 1.58-bit BitNet consistently exhibits smaller performance degradation than full-precision baselines at the same sparsity levels and can tolerate higher structured sparsity before accuracy collapse. Moreover, using our custom sparse tensor core, Sparse-BitNet achieves substantial speedups in both training and inference, reaching up to 1.30X. These results highlight that combining extremely low-bit quantization with semi-structured N:M sparsity is a promising direction for efficient LLMs. Code available at https://github.com/AAzdi/Sparse-BitNet

AI.tldr: Sparse-BitNet combines 1.58-bit quantization with N:M sparsity for efficient LLMs, showing better compatibility than full-precision models and achieving up to 1.30× speedup.
AI.motivation: Semi-structured N:M sparsity and low-bit quantization (like 1.58-bit BitNet) are promising for LLM efficiency but have been studied separately. The paper investigates their interaction and compatibility.
AI.method: Proposes Sparse-BitNet, a unified framework that jointly applies 1.58-bit quantization and dynamic N:M sparsification with stable training. Uses custom sparse tensor cores for acceleration.
AI.result: 1.58-bit BitNet shows smaller performance degradation than full-precision baselines at same sparsity levels, tolerates higher structured sparsity before collapse, and achieves up to 1.30× speedup in training/inference.
AI.conclusion: Combining extremely low-bit quantization with semi-structured N:M sparsity is a promising direction for efficient LLMs, with 1.58-bit BitNet being naturally more compatible with N:M sparsity than full-precision models.

title: PACE: A Personalized Adaptive Curriculum Engine for 9-1-1 Call-taker Training
summary: 9-1-1 call-taking training requires mastery of over a thousand interdependent skills, covering diverse incident types and protocol-specific nuances. A nationwide labor shortage is already straining training capacity, but effective instruction still demands that trainers tailor objectives to each trainee's evolving competencies. This personalization burden is one that current practice cannot scale. Partnering with Metro Nashville Department of Emergency Communications (MNDEC), we propose PACE (Personalized Adaptive Curriculum Engine), a co-pilot system that augments trainer decision-making by (1) maintaining probabilistic beliefs over trainee skill states, (2) modeling individual learning and forgetting dynamics, and (3) recommending training scenarios that balance acquisition of new competencies with retention of existing ones. PACE propagates evidence over a structured skill graph to accelerate diagnostic coverage and applies contextual bandits to select scenarios that target gaps the trainee is prepared to address. Empirical results show that PACE achieves 19.50% faster time-to-competence and 10.95% higher terminal mastery compared to state-of-the-art frameworks. Co-pilot studies with practicing training officers further demonstrate a 95.45% alignment rate between PACE's and experts' pedagogical judgments on real-world cases. Under estimation, PACE cuts turnaround time to merely 34 seconds from 11.58 minutes, up to 95.08% reduction.

AI.tldr: PACE is a personalized adaptive curriculum engine for 9-1-1 call-taker training that uses probabilistic skill modeling and contextual bandits to recommend optimal training scenarios, achieving 19.5% faster competence and 10.95% higher mastery.
AI.motivation: 9-1-1 call-taking training requires mastery of over a thousand interdependent skills, but current training systems cannot scale personalized instruction to address individual trainee competencies amidst nationwide labor shortages.
AI.method: PACE maintains probabilistic beliefs over trainee skill states, models individual learning/forgetting dynamics, propagates evidence over a structured skill graph, and uses contextual bandits to recommend training scenarios that balance new competency acquisition with existing skill retention.
AI.result: PACE achieves 19.50% faster time-to-competence and 10.95% higher terminal mastery compared to state-of-the-art frameworks. Co-pilot studies show 95.45% alignment with expert pedagogical judgments, and reduces turnaround time from 11.58 minutes to 34 seconds (95.08% reduction).
AI.conclusion: PACE effectively addresses the scalability challenge in personalized 9-1-1 call-taker training by augmenting trainer decision-making with AI-driven adaptive curriculum recommendations, significantly improving training efficiency and outcomes.

title: Guidelines for the Annotation and Visualization of Legal Argumentation Structures in Chinese Judicial Decisions
comment: The PDF contains both an English translation and the original Chinese guideline. The first 30 pages present the full English translation, while the remaining 25 pages provide the original Chinese version
summary: This guideline proposes a systematic and operational annotation framework for representing the structure of legal argumentation in judicial decisions. Grounded in theories of legal reasoning and argumentation, the framework aims to reveal the logical organization of judicial reasoning and to provide a reliable data foundation for computational analysis. At the proposition level, the guideline distinguishes four types of propositions: general normative propositions, specific normative propositions, general factual propositions, and specific factual propositions. At the relational level, five types of relations are defined to capture argumentative structures: support, attack, joint, match, and identity. These relations represent positive and negative argumentative connections, conjunctive reasoning structures, the correspondence between legal norms and case facts, and semantic equivalence between propositions. The guideline further specifies formal representation rules and visualization conventions for both basic and nested structures, enabling consistent graphical representation of complex argumentation patterns. In addition, it establishes a standardized annotation workflow and consistency control mechanisms to ensure reproducibility and reliability of the annotated data. By providing a clear conceptual model, formal representation rules, and practical annotation procedures, this guideline offers methodological support for large-scale analysis of judicial reasoning and for future research in legal argument mining, computational modeling of legal reasoning, and AI-assisted legal analysis.

AI.tldr: A systematic annotation framework for representing legal argumentation structure in judicial decisions, with proposition types, argumentative relations, formal representation rules, and standardized workflow for computational analysis.
AI.motivation: To provide a reliable data foundation for computational analysis of judicial reasoning by creating a systematic annotation framework that reveals the logical organization of legal argumentation in judicial decisions.
AI.method: Proposes a two-level annotation framework: at proposition level distinguishes four types (general normative, specific normative, general factual, specific factual); at relational level defines five types of argumentative relations (support, attack, joint, match, identity). Includes formal representation rules, visualization conventions for basic and nested structures, standardized annotation workflow, and consistency control mechanisms.
AI.result: Developed a comprehensive guideline with clear conceptual model, formal representation rules, and practical annotation procedures that enables consistent graphical representation of complex argumentation patterns and ensures reproducibility of annotated data.
AI.conclusion: The guideline provides methodological support for large-scale analysis of judicial reasoning and future research in legal argument mining, computational modeling of legal reasoning, and AI-assisted legal analysis through its systematic annotation framework.

title: Legal interpretation and AI: from expert systems to argumentation and LLMs
summary: AI and Law research has encountered legal interpretation in different ways, in the context of its evolving approaches and methodologies. Research on expert system has focused on legal knowledge engineering, with the goal of ensuring that human-generated interpretations can be precisely transferred into knowledge-bases, to be consistently applied. Research on argumentation has aimed at representing the structure of interpretive arguments, as well as their dialectical interactions, to assess of the acceptability of interpretive claims within argumentation frameworks. Research on machine learning has focused on the automated generation of interpretive suggestions and arguments, through general and specialised language models, now being increasingly deployed in legal practice.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys how AI and Law research has approached legal interpretation through three main paradigms: expert systems for knowledge engineering, argumentation frameworks for representing interpretive arguments, and machine learning for automated generation of interpretive suggestions.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of how different AI methodologies have been applied to the complex problem of legal interpretation, highlighting the evolution of approaches in the AI and Law field.
AI.method: The paper employs a survey methodology, analyzing three key research streams: 1) Expert systems focusing on legal knowledge engineering to transfer human interpretations into knowledge-bases, 2) Argumentation research representing interpretive argument structures and dialectical interactions within argumentation frameworks, and 3) Machine learning approaches using general and specialized language models for automated generation of interpretive suggestions.
AI.result: The analysis reveals distinct approaches to legal interpretation across AI paradigms: expert systems aim for precise transfer of human interpretations, argumentation frameworks focus on representing argument structures and assessing claim acceptability, and machine learning enables automated generation of interpretive suggestions that are increasingly deployed in legal practice.
AI.conclusion: AI and Law research has developed diverse methodologies for addressing legal interpretation, with each approach offering different strengths - from precise knowledge engineering to argument representation and automated generation - reflecting the field's evolution and growing practical application in legal contexts.

title: Transducing Language Models
summary: Modern language models define distributions over strings, but downstream tasks often require different output formats. For instance, a model that generates byte-pair strings does not directly produce word-level predictions, and a DNA model does not directly produce amino-acid sequences. In such cases, a deterministic string-to-string transformation can convert the model's output to the desired form. This is a familiar pattern in probability theory: applying a function $f$ to a random variable $X\sim p$ yields a transformed random variable $f(X)$ with an induced distribution. While such transformations are occasionally used in language modeling, prior work does not treat them as yielding new, fully functional language models. We formalize this perspective and introduce a general framework for language models derived from deterministic string-to-string transformations. We focus on transformations representable as finite-state transducers -- a commonly used state-machine abstraction for efficient string-to-string mappings. We develop algorithms that compose a language model with an FST to *marginalize* over source strings mapping to a given target, propagating probabilities through the transducer without altering model parameters and enabling *conditioning* on transformed outputs. We present an exact algorithm, an efficient approximation, and a theoretical analysis. We conduct experiments in three domains: converting language models from tokens to bytes, from tokens to words, and from DNA to amino acids. These experiments demonstrate inference-time adaptation of pretrained language models to match application-specific output requirements.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework for creating new language models by applying deterministic string-to-string transformations (finite-state transducers) to existing language models, enabling inference-time adaptation to different output formats without retraining.
AI.motivation: Language models produce outputs in specific formats (e.g., byte-pair strings, DNA sequences), but downstream applications often require different formats (e.g., word-level predictions, amino-acid sequences). Current approaches don't treat these transformations as yielding fully functional new language models.
AI.method: The authors formalize a framework where language models can be derived from deterministic string-to-string transformations, focusing on finite-state transducers (FSTs). They develop algorithms that compose a language model with an FST to marginalize over source strings mapping to a given target, propagating probabilities through the transducer without altering model parameters. They present both exact and approximate algorithms with theoretical analysis.
AI.result: Experiments in three domains demonstrate successful inference-time adaptation: converting language models from tokens to bytes, from tokens to words, and from DNA to amino acids. The framework enables pretrained language models to match application-specific output requirements without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic string-to-string transformations can be used to create new, fully functional language models from existing ones. The finite-state transducer framework provides efficient algorithms for marginalization and conditioning on transformed outputs, enabling flexible inference-time adaptation of pretrained models to various output formats.

title: Judge Reliability Harness: Stress Testing the Reliability of LLM Judges
comment: Accepted at Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond Workshop at ICLR 2026 - April 26, 2026, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
summary: We present the Judge Reliability Harness, an open source library for constructing validation suites that test the reliability of LLM judges. As LLM based scoring is widely deployed in AI benchmarks, more tooling is needed to efficiently assess the reliability of these methods. Given a benchmark dataset and an LLM judge configuration, the harness generates reliability tests that evaluate both binary judgment accuracy and ordinal grading performance for free-response and agentic task formats. We evaluate four state-of-the-art judges across four benchmarks spanning safety, persuasion, misuse, and agentic behavior, and find meaningful variation in performance across models and perturbation types, highlighting opportunities to improve the robustness of LLM judges. No judge that we evaluated is uniformly reliable across benchmarks using our harness. For example, our preliminary experiments on judges revealed consistency issues as measured by accuracy in judging another LLM's ability to complete a task due to simple text formatting changes, paraphrasing, changes in verbosity, and flipping the ground truth label in LLM-produced responses. The code for this tool is available at: https://github.com/RANDCorporation/judge-reliability-harness

AI.tldr: The Judge Reliability Harness is an open-source library for testing LLM judge reliability across benchmarks, revealing performance variations and consistency issues with text perturbations.
AI.motivation: LLM-based scoring is widely deployed in AI benchmarks, but there's insufficient tooling to efficiently assess the reliability of these scoring methods. The need exists for systematic evaluation of LLM judges' robustness across different task formats and perturbation types.
AI.method: The harness generates reliability tests that evaluate both binary judgment accuracy and ordinal grading performance for free-response and agentic task formats. Given a benchmark dataset and LLM judge configuration, it systematically tests judges across various perturbation types including text formatting changes, paraphrasing, verbosity changes, and ground truth label flipping.
AI.result: Evaluation of four state-of-the-art judges across four benchmarks (safety, persuasion, misuse, and agentic behavior) revealed meaningful variation in performance across models and perturbation types. No evaluated judge was uniformly reliable across benchmarks. Preliminary experiments showed consistency issues with accuracy affected by simple text formatting changes, paraphrasing, verbosity changes, and ground truth label flipping.
AI.conclusion: The Judge Reliability Harness provides essential tooling for assessing LLM judge reliability, highlighting significant opportunities to improve robustness. The findings demonstrate that current LLM judges are not uniformly reliable and are sensitive to various text perturbations, emphasizing the need for more robust evaluation methods in AI benchmarking.

title: Diffusion LLMs can think EoS-by-EoS
summary: Diffusion LLMs have been proposed as an alternative to autoregressive LLMs, excelling especially at complex reasoning tasks with interdependent sub-goals. Curiously, this is particularly true if the generation length, i.e., the number of tokens the model has to output, is set to a much higher value than is required for providing the correct answer to the task, and the model pads its answer with end-of-sequence (EoS) tokens. We hypothesize that diffusion models think EoS-by-EoS, that is, they use the representations of EoS tokens as a hidden scratchpad, which allows them to solve harder reasoning problems. We experiment with the diffusion models LLaDA1.5, LLaDA2.0-mini, and Dream-v0 on the tasks Addition, Entity Tracking, and Sudoku. In a controlled prompting experiment, we confirm that adding EoS tokens improves the LLMs' reasoning capabilities. To further verify whether they serve as space for hidden computations, we patch the hidden states of the EoS tokens with those of a counterfactual generation, which frequently changes the generated output to the counterfactual. The success of the causal intervention underscores that the EoS tokens, which one may expect to be devoid of meaning, carry information on the problem to solve. The behavioral experiments and the causal interventions indicate that diffusion LLMs can indeed think EoS-by-EoS.

AI.tldr: Diffusion LLMs use end-of-sequence (EoS) tokens as hidden scratchpads for complex reasoning, with performance improving when generation length exceeds required answer length.
AI.motivation: To understand why diffusion LLMs perform better on complex reasoning tasks when generating more tokens than needed, particularly investigating the role of EoS tokens as potential computational scratchpads.
AI.method: Experiments with diffusion models (LLaDA1.5, LLaDA2.0-mini, Dream-v0) on Addition, Entity Tracking, and Sudoku tasks; controlled prompting to test EoS token effects; causal interventions by patching EoS token hidden states with counterfactual representations.
AI.result: Adding EoS tokens improves reasoning capabilities; patching EoS token hidden states frequently changes output to counterfactual, demonstrating EoS tokens carry meaningful computational information.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion LLMs use EoS tokens as hidden scratchpads ("think EoS-by-EoS"), enabling them to solve complex reasoning problems by leveraging these tokens for intermediate computations.

title: Dissociating Direct Access from Inference in AI Introspection
summary: Introspection is a foundational cognitive ability, but its mechanism is not well understood. Recent work has shown that AI models can introspect. We study their mechanism of introspection, first extensively replicating Lindsey et al. (2025)'s thought injection detection paradigm in large open-source models. We show that these models detect injected representations via two separable mechanisms: (i) probability-matching (inferring from perceived anomaly of the prompt) and (ii) direct access to internal states. The direct access mechanism is content-agnostic: models detect that an anomaly occurred but cannot reliably identify its semantic content. The two model classes we study confabulate injected concepts that are high-frequency and concrete (e.g., "apple'"); for them correct concept guesses typically require significantly more tokens. This content-agnostic introspective mechanism is consistent with leading theories in philosophy and psychology.

AI.tldr: AI models detect thought injections via two mechanisms: probability-matching (inferring from prompt anomalies) and content-agnostic direct access to internal states, with models often confabulating high-frequency concrete concepts.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanisms of introspection in AI models, particularly how they detect injected representations, building on recent work showing AI models can introspect and Lindsey et al.'s thought injection detection paradigm.
AI.method: Extensive replication of Lindsey et al.'s (2025) thought injection detection paradigm in large open-source models, analyzing how models detect injected representations through probability-matching and direct access to internal states.
AI.result: Models detect injected representations via two separable mechanisms: probability-matching (inferring from perceived prompt anomalies) and direct access to internal states. The direct access mechanism is content-agnostic - models detect anomalies but cannot reliably identify semantic content. Models confabulate high-frequency, concrete concepts (e.g., "apple"), and correct concept guesses typically require significantly more tokens.
AI.conclusion: The content-agnostic introspective mechanism found in AI models aligns with leading theories in philosophy and psychology about introspection mechanisms.

title: Distilling Formal Logic into Neural Spaces: A Kernel Alignment Approach for Signal Temporal Logic
summary: We introduce a framework for learning continuous neural representations of formal specifications by distilling the geometry of their semantics into a latent space. Existing approaches rely either on symbolic kernels -- which preserve behavioural semantics but are computationally prohibitive, anchor-dependent, and non-invertible -- or on syntax-based neural embeddings that fail to capture underlying structures. Our method bridges this gap: using a teacher-student setup, we distill a symbolic robustness kernel into a Transformer encoder. Unlike standard contrastive methods, we supervise the model with a continuous, kernel-weighted geometric alignment objective that penalizes errors in proportion to their semantic discrepancies. Once trained, the encoder produces embeddings in a single forward pass, effectively mimicking the kernel's logic at a fraction of its computational cost. We apply our framework to Signal Temporal Logic (STL), demonstrating that the resulting neural representations faithfully preserve the semantic similarity of STL formulae, accurately predict robustness and constraint satisfaction, and remain intrinsically invertible. Our proposed approach enables highly efficient, scalable neuro-symbolic reasoning and formula reconstruction without repeated kernel computation at runtime.

AI.tldr: A framework for learning continuous neural representations of formal specifications by distilling symbolic robustness kernels into Transformer encoders, enabling efficient neuro-symbolic reasoning with preserved semantic geometry.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for formal specification representation have limitations: symbolic kernels preserve behavioral semantics but are computationally prohibitive, anchor-dependent, and non-invertible, while syntax-based neural embeddings fail to capture underlying semantic structures. There is a need to bridge this gap between symbolic and neural approaches.
AI.method: Uses a teacher-student setup to distill a symbolic robustness kernel into a Transformer encoder. Employs a continuous, kernel-weighted geometric alignment objective that penalizes errors proportionally to semantic discrepancies, unlike standard contrastive methods. Once trained, the encoder produces embeddings in a single forward pass, mimicking kernel logic at reduced computational cost.
AI.result: Applied to Signal Temporal Logic (STL), the neural representations faithfully preserve semantic similarity of STL formulae, accurately predict robustness and constraint satisfaction, and remain intrinsically invertible. The approach enables highly efficient, scalable neuro-symbolic reasoning and formula reconstruction without repeated kernel computation at runtime.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully bridges the gap between symbolic and neural approaches for formal specification representation, providing computationally efficient neural embeddings that preserve semantic geometry while maintaining invertibility for formula reconstruction.

title: Distributed Partial Information Puzzles: Examining Common Ground Construction Under Epistemic Asymmetry
summary: Establishing common ground, a shared set of beliefs and mutually recognized facts, is fundamental to collaboration, yet remains a challenge for current AI systems, especially in multimodal, multiparty settings, where the collaborators bring different information to the table. We introduce the Distributed Partial Information Puzzle (DPIP), a collaborative construction task that elicits rich multimodal communication under epistemic asymmetry. We present a multimodal dataset of these interactions, annotated and temporally aligned across speech, gesture, and action modalities to support reasoning over propositional content and belief dynamics. We then evaluate two paradigms for modeling common ground (CG): (1) state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), prompted to infer shared beliefs from multimodal updates, and (2) an axiomatic pipeline grounded in Dynamic Epistemic Logic (DEL) that incrementally performs the same task. Results on the annotated DPIP data indicate that it poses a challenge to modern LLMs' abilities to track both task progression and belief state.

AI.tldr: DPIP is a multimodal collaborative construction task that creates epistemic asymmetry to study common ground formation, with results showing LLMs struggle with belief state tracking despite multimodal inputs.
AI.motivation: Current AI systems struggle with establishing common ground in multimodal, multiparty collaborative settings where participants have different information (epistemic asymmetry), which is fundamental to effective collaboration.
AI.method: Introduced Distributed Partial Information Puzzle (DPIP) - a collaborative construction task that elicits rich multimodal communication. Created a multimodal dataset with temporal alignment across speech, gesture, and action modalities. Evaluated two paradigms: (1) state-of-the-art LLMs prompted to infer shared beliefs from multimodal updates, and (2) an axiomatic pipeline based on Dynamic Epistemic Logic (DEL) for incremental belief tracking.
AI.result: DPIP poses a significant challenge to modern LLMs' abilities to track both task progression and belief state, despite their access to multimodal inputs. The DEL-based pipeline provides a structured alternative for belief state tracking in epistemic asymmetry scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Establishing common ground in multimodal, multiparty settings with epistemic asymmetry remains challenging for current AI systems, with LLMs showing limitations in belief state tracking that may require more structured approaches like DEL-based methods.

title: Balancing Coverage and Draft Latency in Vocabulary Trimming for Faster Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates inference for Large Language Models by using a lightweight draft model to propose candidate tokens that are verified in parallel by a larger target model. Prior work shows that the draft model often dominates speculative decoding latency, since it generates tokens sequentially and incurs high cost from its language modeling head as vocabulary size grows. This exposes a fundamental trade-off in draft model design: larger vocabularies improve token coverage and agreement with the target model, but incur higher draft latency, while smaller vocabularies reduce latency at the risk of missing tokens required for accurate draft generation. We address this trade-off through vocabulary trimming for draft models, motivated by the observation that domain-specific workloads use only a small fraction of the full vocabulary. We cast draft vocabulary selection as a constrained optimization problem that balances token coverage and draft latency. Coverage is computed over assistant responses in the training data, while latency is estimated using architecture-aware FLOPs that capture the cost of the language modeling head as a function of vocabulary size. We optimize a utility function with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator to efficiently explore the coverage-latency Pareto frontier under a minimum coverage constraint. Experiments show improved speculative decoding throughput while reducing draft vocabularies by up to 97% with high coverage. On domain-specific tasks, we achieve up to 16% latency reduction and 20% throughput improvement, and up to 6.7% throughput gains on diverse out-of-distribution tasks.

AI.tldr: Vocabulary trimming for draft models in speculative decoding improves throughput by reducing draft latency while maintaining token coverage, achieving up to 20% throughput gains on domain-specific tasks.
AI.motivation: There's a fundamental trade-off in draft model design for speculative decoding: larger vocabularies improve token coverage and agreement with the target model but increase draft latency, while smaller vocabularies reduce latency but risk missing tokens needed for accurate draft generation. Domain-specific workloads use only a small fraction of the full vocabulary, creating an opportunity for optimization.
AI.method: The paper proposes vocabulary trimming for draft models by casting draft vocabulary selection as a constrained optimization problem. Coverage is computed over assistant responses in training data, while latency is estimated using architecture-aware FLOPs that capture the cost of the language modeling head as a function of vocabulary size. A Tree-structured Parzen Estimator optimizes a utility function to efficiently explore the coverage-latency Pareto frontier under a minimum coverage constraint.
AI.result: Experiments show improved speculative decoding throughput while reducing draft vocabularies by up to 97% with high coverage. On domain-specific tasks, the method achieves up to 16% latency reduction and 20% throughput improvement, and up to 6.7% throughput gains on diverse out-of-distribution tasks.
AI.conclusion: Vocabulary trimming effectively addresses the draft model design trade-off in speculative decoding, demonstrating that significant vocabulary reduction (up to 97%) can be achieved while maintaining coverage, leading to substantial throughput improvements across both domain-specific and out-of-distribution tasks.

title: Towards Provably Unbiased LLM Judges via Bias-Bounded Evaluation
summary: As AI models progress beyond simple chatbots into more complex workflows, we draw ever closer to the event horizon beyond which AI systems will be utilized in autonomous, self-maintaining feedback loops. Any autonomous AI system will depend on automated, verifiable rewards and feedback; in settings where ground truth is sparse or non-deterministic, one practical source of such rewards is an LLM-as-a-Judge. Although LLM judges continue to improve, the literature has yet to introduce systems capable of enforcing standards with strong guarantees, particularly when bias vectors are unknown or adversarially discovered. To remedy this issue, we propose average bias-boundedness (A-BB), an algorithmic framework which formally guarantees reductions of harm/impact as a result of any measurable bias in an LLM judge. Evaluating on Arena-Hard-Auto with four LLM judges, we achieve (tau=0.5, delta=0.01) bias-bounded guarantees while retaining 61-99% correlation with original rankings across formatting and schematic bias settings, with most judge-bias combinations exceeding 80%. The code to reproduce our findings is available at https://github.com/penfever/bias-bounded-evaluation.

AI.tldr: Proposes average bias-boundedness (A-BB) framework to provide formal guarantees against bias in LLM-as-a-Judge systems for autonomous AI feedback loops.
AI.motivation: As AI systems move toward autonomous feedback loops, they require automated, verifiable rewards. LLM-as-a-Judge provides rewards when ground truth is sparse, but current systems lack strong guarantees against bias, especially when bias vectors are unknown or adversarial.
AI.method: Introduces average bias-boundedness (A-BB) algorithmic framework that formally guarantees reductions of harm/impact from any measurable bias in an LLM judge. Evaluated on Arena-Hard-Auto with four LLM judges.
AI.result: Achieved (τ=0.5, δ=0.01) bias-bounded guarantees while retaining 61-99% correlation with original rankings across formatting and schematic bias settings, with most judge-bias combinations exceeding 80% correlation.
AI.conclusion: The A-BB framework provides a practical solution for ensuring bias-bounded guarantees in LLM-as-a-Judge systems, addressing a critical gap in autonomous AI feedback loops where verifiable rewards are needed.

title: VietJobs: A Vietnamese Job Advertisement Dataset
summary: VietJobs is the first large-scale, publicly available corpus of Vietnamese job advertisements, comprising 48,092 postings and over 15 million words collected from all 34 provinces and municipalities across Vietnam. The dataset provides extensive linguistic and structured information, including job titles, categories, salaries, skills, and employment conditions, covering 16 occupational domains and multiple employment types (full-time, part-time, and internship). Designed to support research in natural language processing and labour market analytics, VietJobs captures substantial linguistic, regional, and socio-economic diversity. We benchmark several generative large language models (LLMs) on two core tasks: job category classification and salary estimation. Instruction-tuned models such as Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-SEA-LION-v3-8B-IT demonstrate notable gains under few-shot and fine-tuned settings, while highlighting challenges in multilingual and Vietnamese-specific modelling for structured labour market prediction. VietJobs establishes a new benchmark for Vietnamese NLP and offers a valuable foundation for future research on recruitment language, socio-economic representation, and AI-driven labour market analysis. All code and resources are available at: https://github.com/VinNLP/VietJobs.

AI.tldr: VietJobs is the first large-scale Vietnamese job advertisement corpus with 48K postings covering all 34 provinces, supporting NLP and labor market research with benchmarks for job classification and salary estimation.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of large-scale, publicly available Vietnamese job advertisement datasets for NLP research and labor market analytics, capturing Vietnam's linguistic, regional, and socio-economic diversity.
AI.method: Collected 48,092 job postings from all 34 Vietnamese provinces/municipalities, annotated with job titles, categories, salaries, skills, and conditions. Benchmarked LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-SEA-LION-v3-8B-IT) on job category classification and salary estimation tasks under few-shot and fine-tuned settings.
AI.result: Instruction-tuned LLMs showed notable performance gains on classification and estimation tasks, while revealing challenges in multilingual and Vietnamese-specific modeling for structured labor market prediction.
AI.conclusion: VietJobs establishes a new benchmark for Vietnamese NLP and provides a valuable foundation for research on recruitment language, socio-economic representation, and AI-driven labor market analysis, with all resources publicly available.

title: The Spike, the Sparse and the Sink: Anatomy of Massive Activations and Attention Sinks
summary: We study two recurring phenomena in Transformer language models: massive activations, in which a small number of tokens exhibit extreme outliers in a few channels, and attention sinks, in which certain tokens attract disproportionate attention mass regardless of semantic relevance. Prior work observes that these phenomena frequently co-occur and often involve the same tokens, but their functional roles and causal relationship remain unclear. Through systematic experiments, we show that the co-occurrence is largely an architectural artifact of modern Transformer design, and that the two phenomena serve related but distinct functions. Massive activations operate globally: they induce near-constant hidden representations that persist across layers, effectively functioning as implicit parameters of the model. Attention sinks operate locally: they modulate attention outputs across heads and bias individual heads toward short-range dependencies. We identify the pre-norm configuration as the key choice that enables the co-occurrence, and show that ablating it causes the two phenomena to decouple.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the relationship between massive activations and attention sinks in Transformers, showing they are architectural artifacts that serve distinct functions: massive activations create global persistent representations while attention sinks modulate local attention patterns.
AI.motivation: To understand the functional roles and causal relationship between two recurring phenomena in Transformer language models: massive activations (extreme outliers in few channels) and attention sinks (tokens attracting disproportionate attention mass), which frequently co-occur but whose relationship remains unclear.
AI.method: Systematic experiments analyzing Transformer architectures, identifying the pre-norm configuration as key to enabling co-occurrence, and ablating it to decouple the phenomena and study their distinct functions.
AI.result: Massive activations operate globally by inducing near-constant hidden representations that persist across layers, functioning as implicit model parameters. Attention sinks operate locally by modulating attention outputs across heads and biasing individual heads toward short-range dependencies. The pre-norm configuration enables their co-occurrence, and ablating it causes decoupling.
AI.conclusion: The co-occurrence of massive activations and attention sinks is largely an architectural artifact of modern Transformer design, with the two phenomena serving related but distinct functions: global persistent representations vs. local attention modulation.

title: Oral to Web: Digitizing 'Zero Resource'Languages of Bangladesh
summary: We present the Multilingual Cloud Corpus, the first national-scale, parallel, multimodal linguistic dataset of Bangladesh's ethnic and indigenous languages. Despite being home to approximately 40 minority languages spanning four language families, Bangladesh has lacked a systematic, cross-family digital corpus for these predominantly oral, computationally "zero resource" varieties, 14 of which are classified as endangered. Our corpus comprises 85792 structured textual entries, each containing a Bengali stimulus text, an English translation, and an IPA transcription, together with approximately 107 hours of transcribed audio recordings, covering 42 language varieties from the Tibeto-Burman, Indo-European, Austro-Asiatic, and Dravidian families, plus two genetically unclassified languages. The data were collected through systematic fieldwork over 90 days across nine districts of Bangladesh, involving 16 data collectors, 77 speakers, and 43 validators, following a predefined elicitation template of 2224 unique items organized at three levels of linguistic granularity: isolated lexical items (475 words across 22 semantic domains), grammatical constructions (887 sentences across 21 categories including verbal conjugation paradigms), and directed speech (862 prompts across 46 conversational scenarios). Post-field processing included IPA transcription by 10 linguists with independent adjudication by 6 reviewers. The complete dataset is publicly accessible through the Multilingual Cloud platform (multiling.cloud), providing searchable access to annotated audio and textual data for all documented varieties. We describe the corpus design, fieldwork methodology, dataset structure, and per-language coverage, and discuss implications for endangered language documentation, low-resource NLP, and digital preservation in linguistically diverse developing countries.

AI.tldr: The Multilingual Cloud Corpus is Bangladesh's first national-scale parallel multimodal dataset covering 42 ethnic/indigenous languages from four language families, featuring 85,792 textual entries with Bengali stimuli, English translations, IPA transcriptions, and 107 hours of audio recordings.
AI.motivation: Bangladesh has approximately 40 minority languages spanning four language families, many of which are oral, computationally "zero resource" varieties with 14 classified as endangered. There was a lack of systematic, cross-family digital corpus for these languages, hindering documentation, preservation, and computational research.
AI.method: Systematic 90-day fieldwork across nine districts involving 16 data collectors, 77 speakers, and 43 validators using a predefined elicitation template of 2,224 unique items organized at three linguistic levels: isolated lexical items (475 words across 22 semantic domains), grammatical constructions (887 sentences across 21 categories), and directed speech (862 prompts across 46 conversational scenarios). Post-field processing included IPA transcription by 10 linguists with independent adjudication by 6 reviewers.
AI.result: Created a corpus of 85,792 structured textual entries (each with Bengali stimulus, English translation, and IPA transcription) and approximately 107 hours of transcribed audio recordings covering 42 language varieties from Tibeto-Burman, Indo-European, Austro-Asiatic, and Dravidian families, plus two genetically unclassified languages. The complete dataset is publicly accessible through the Multilingual Cloud platform (multiling.cloud).
AI.conclusion: This first national-scale parallel multimodal corpus for Bangladesh's ethnic and indigenous languages provides a valuable resource for endangered language documentation, low-resource NLP research, and digital preservation in linguistically diverse developing countries, addressing the critical gap in systematic cross-family linguistic data.

title: A theoretical model of dynamical grammatical gender shifting based on set-valued set function
summary: This study investigates the diverse characteristics of nouns, focusing on both semantic (e.g., countable/uncountable) and morphosyntactic (e.g., masculine/feminine) distinctions. We explore inter-word variations for gender markers in noun morphology. Grammatical gender shift is a widespread phenomenon in languages around the world. The aim is to uncover through a formal model the underlying patterns governing the variation of lexemes. To this end, we propose a new computational component dedicated to pairing items with morphological templates (e.g., the result of a generated item-template pair: (funas, $\{N, +SG, -PL, -M, +F, -COL, +SING\}$), with its spell-out form: $ð$a-funast 'cow'). This process is formally represented by the Template-Based and Modular Cognitive model. This proposed model, defined by a set-valued set function $h : \mathscr{P}(M) \rightarrow \mathscr{P}(M)$, predicts the nonlinear dynamic mapping of lexical items onto morphological templates. By applying this formalism, we present a unified framework for understanding the complexities of morphological markings across languages. Through empirical observations, we demonstrate how these shifts, as well as non-gender shifts, arise during lexical changes, especially in Riffian. Our model posits that these variant markings emerge due to template shifts occurring during word and meaning's formation. By formally demonstrating that conversion is applicable to noun-to-noun derivation, we challenge and broaden the conventional view of word formation. This mathematical model not only contributes to a deeper understanding of morphosyntactic variation but also offers potential applications in other fields requiring precise modelling of linguistic patterns.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a computational model for analyzing noun characteristics, focusing on semantic and morphosyntactic distinctions, particularly gender variation in languages.
AI.motivation: To understand the underlying patterns governing variation in noun lexemes, particularly grammatical gender shifts and other morphological variations that occur across languages, with specific interest in phenomena like those observed in Riffian.
AI.method: Developed a Template-Based and Modular Cognitive model using a set-valued set function h: 𝒫(M) → 𝒫(M) to predict nonlinear dynamic mapping of lexical items onto morphological templates, enabling computational pairing of items with morphological templates.
AI.result: The model successfully demonstrates how gender shifts and non-gender shifts arise during lexical changes, provides a unified framework for understanding morphological markings across languages, and shows that conversion applies to noun-to-noun derivation, challenging conventional views of word formation.
AI.conclusion: The mathematical model offers deeper understanding of morphosyntactic variation and has potential applications in other fields requiring precise modeling of linguistic patterns, while broadening perspectives on word formation processes.

title: Med-V1: Small Language Models for Zero-shot and Scalable Biomedical Evidence Attribution
summary: Assessing whether an article supports an assertion is essential for hallucination detection and claim verification. While large language models (LLMs) have the potential to automate this task, achieving strong performance requires frontier models such as GPT-5 that are prohibitively expensive to deploy at scale. To efficiently perform biomedical evidence attribution, we present Med-V1, a family of small language models with only three billion parameters. Trained on high-quality synthetic data newly developed in this study, Med-V1 substantially outperforms (+27.0% to +71.3%) its base models on five biomedical benchmarks unified into a verification format. Despite its smaller size, Med-V1 performs comparably to frontier LLMs such as GPT-5, along with high-quality explanations for its predictions. We use Med-V1 to conduct a first-of-its-kind use case study that quantifies hallucinations in LLM-generated answers under different citation instructions. Results show that the format instruction strongly affects citation validity and hallucination, with GPT-5 generating more claims but exhibiting hallucination rates similar to GPT-4o. Additionally, we present a second use case showing that Med-V1 can automatically identify high-stakes evidence misattributions in clinical practice guidelines, revealing potentially negative public health impacts that are otherwise challenging to identify at scale. Overall, Med-V1 provides an efficient and accurate lightweight alternative to frontier LLMs for practical and real-world applications in biomedical evidence attribution and verification tasks. Med-V1 is available at https://github.com/ncbi-nlp/Med-V1.

AI.tldr: Med-V1 is a 3B-parameter biomedical evidence attribution model that matches frontier LLM performance while being much more efficient, trained on synthetic data for verification tasks.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs like GPT-5 are too expensive for scalable biomedical evidence attribution, which is essential for hallucination detection and claim verification in biomedical contexts.
AI.method: Developed Med-V1 family of small language models (3B parameters) trained on high-quality synthetic data specifically created for biomedical verification tasks, unifying five biomedical benchmarks into verification format.
AI.result: Med-V1 outperforms base models by 27.0-71.3% on biomedical benchmarks, performs comparably to frontier LLMs like GPT-5, provides high-quality explanations, and successfully identifies citation validity patterns and clinical guideline misattributions in use cases.
AI.conclusion: Med-V1 offers an efficient, accurate lightweight alternative to expensive frontier LLMs for practical biomedical evidence attribution and verification applications, with demonstrated real-world utility in hallucination quantification and clinical guideline analysis.

title: PersianPunc: A Large-Scale Dataset and BERT-Based Approach for Persian Punctuation Restoration
summary: Punctuation restoration is essential for improving the readability and downstream utility of automatic speech recognition (ASR) outputs, yet remains underexplored for Persian despite its importance. We introduce PersianPunc, a large-scale, high-quality dataset of 17 million samples for Persian punctuation restoration, constructed through systematic aggregation and filtering of existing textual resources. We formulate punctuation restoration as a token-level sequence labeling task and fine-tune ParsBERT to achieve strong performance. Through comparative evaluation, we demonstrate that while large language models can perform punctuation restoration, they suffer from critical limitations: over-correction tendencies that introduce undesired edits beyond punctuation insertion (particularly problematic for speech-to-text pipelines) and substantially higher computational requirements. Our lightweight BERT-based approach achieves a macro-averaged F1 score of 91.33% on our test set while maintaining efficiency suitable for real-time applications. We make our dataset (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MohammadJRanjbar/persian-punctuation-restoration) and model (https://huggingface.co/MohammadJRanjbar/parsbert-persian-punctuation) publicly available to facilitate future research in Persian NLP and provide a scalable framework applicable to other morphologically rich, low-resource languages.

AI.tldr: PersianPunc: A large-scale Persian punctuation restoration dataset (17M samples) and BERT-based model that outperforms LLMs by avoiding over-correction while maintaining real-time efficiency.
AI.motivation: Punctuation restoration is crucial for improving ASR output readability and downstream utility, but remains underexplored for Persian despite its importance, creating a gap for this morphologically rich, low-resource language.
AI.method: Created PersianPunc dataset through systematic aggregation/filtering of existing textual resources (17M samples), formulated punctuation restoration as token-level sequence labeling, and fine-tuned ParsBERT for the task.
AI.result: BERT-based approach achieved 91.33% macro-averaged F1 score on test set, outperforming LLMs which suffer from over-correction (introducing undesired edits beyond punctuation) and higher computational requirements.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight BERT-based approach provides efficient, accurate punctuation restoration suitable for real-time applications, with publicly available dataset and model to advance Persian NLP and provide framework for other low-resource languages.

title: A Multilingual Human Annotated Corpus of Original and Easy-to-Read Texts to Support Access to Democratic Participatory Processes
summary: Being able to understand information is a key factor for a self-determined life and society. It is also very important for participating in democratic processes. The study of automatic text simplification is often limited by the availability of high quality material for the training and evaluation on automatic simplifiers. This is true for English, but more so for less resourced languages like Spanish, Catalan and Italian. In order to fill this gap, we present a corpus of original texts for these 3 languages, with high quality simplification produced by human experts in text simplification. It was developed within the iDEM project to assess the impact of Easy-to-Read (E2R) language for democratic participation. The original texts were compiled from domains related to this topic. The corpus includes different text types, selected based on relevance, copyright availability, and ethical standards. All texts were simplified to E2R level. The corpus is particularity valuable because it includes the first annotated corpus of its kind for the Catalan language. It also represents a noteworthy contribution for Spanish and Italian, offering high-quality, human-annotated language resources that are rarely available in these domains. The corpus will be made freely accessible to the public.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multilingual corpus of original texts in Spanish, Catalan, and Italian with high-quality human expert simplifications to Easy-to-Read level, developed to support democratic participation research.
AI.motivation: Text comprehension is crucial for self-determination and democratic participation, but automatic text simplification research is limited by the lack of high-quality training/evaluation data, especially for less-resourced languages like Spanish, Catalan, and Italian.
AI.method: Created a corpus of original texts from domains relevant to democratic participation, selected based on relevance, copyright availability, and ethical standards. All texts were simplified to Easy-to-Read level by human experts in text simplification within the iDEM project.
AI.result: Produced the first annotated corpus of its kind for Catalan, and a significant contribution for Spanish and Italian - high-quality, human-annotated language resources rarely available in these domains. The corpus includes different text types and will be made freely accessible.
AI.conclusion: The corpus fills a critical gap in resources for automatic text simplification research in less-resourced languages, supporting democratic participation studies and providing valuable training/evaluation data for Spanish, Catalan, and Italian text simplification systems.

title: Exploring the potential and limitations of Model Merging for Multi-Domain Adaptation in ASR
comment: submitted for review for INTERSPEECH2026 conference
summary: Model merging is a scalable alternative to multi-task training that combines the capabilities of multiple specialised models into a single model. This is particularly attractive for large speech foundation models, which are typically adapted through domain-specific fine-tuning, resulting in multiple customised checkpoints, for which repeating full fine-tuning when new data becomes available is computationally prohibitive. In this work, we study model merging for multi-domain ASR and benchmark 11 merging algorithms for 10 European Portuguese domains, evaluating in-domain accuracy, robustness under distribution shift, as well as English and multilingual performance. We further propose BoostedTSV-M, a new merging algorithm based on TSV-M that mitigates rank collapse via singular-value boosting and improves numerical stability. Overall, our approach outperforms full fine-tuning on European Portuguese while preserving out-of-distribution generalisation in a single model.

AI.tldr: Model merging for multi-domain ASR outperforms full fine-tuning for European Portuguese while maintaining generalization, with a new BoostedTSV-M algorithm improving stability.
AI.motivation: Model merging offers a scalable alternative to computationally expensive multi-task training for large speech foundation models, especially when dealing with multiple domain-specific fine-tuned checkpoints where repeating full fine-tuning for new data is prohibitive.
AI.method: Benchmarked 11 merging algorithms for 10 European Portuguese domains, evaluating in-domain accuracy, robustness under distribution shift, and English/multilingual performance. Proposed BoostedTSV-M, a new algorithm based on TSV-M that mitigates rank collapse via singular-value boosting and improves numerical stability.
AI.result: Overall approach outperforms full fine-tuning on European Portuguese while preserving out-of-distribution generalization in a single model. BoostedTSV-M effectively addresses rank collapse and stability issues.
AI.conclusion: Model merging is an effective scalable solution for multi-domain ASR that surpasses full fine-tuning performance while maintaining generalization capabilities, with BoostedTSV-M providing improved algorithmic stability.

title: DiSCTT: Consensus-Guided Self-Curriculum for Efficient Test-Time Adaptation in Reasoning
summary: Test-time adaptation offers a promising avenue for improving reasoning performance in large language models without additional supervision, but existing approaches often apply a uniform optimization objective across all inputs, leading to inefficient or unstable adaptation on heterogeneous reasoning problems. We propose DiSCTT, a difficulty-aware, consensus-guided self-curriculum framework that dynamically allocates test-time optimization strategies based on instance-level epistemic uncertainty estimated from agreement among sampled reasoning trajectories. Inputs with high consensus are consolidated via supervised fine-tuning using majority-agreed solutions as pseudo-labels, while low-consensus inputs are optimized via reinforcement learning with a consensus-regularized objective that encourages diversity under relevance constraints. Across a broad suite of mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks, DiSCTT consistently outperforms strong test-time adaptation baselines, achieving higher accuracy with reduced variance and substantially lower computation and wall-clock training times. These results demonstrate that explicitly accounting for instance difficulty and uncertainty enables more stable, efficient, and effective test-time adaptation for reasoning models.

AI.tldr: DiSCTT is a difficulty-aware, consensus-guided self-curriculum framework for test-time adaptation in LLMs that dynamically allocates optimization strategies based on instance-level epistemic uncertainty estimated from reasoning trajectory agreement.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time adaptation approaches apply uniform optimization objectives across all inputs, leading to inefficient or unstable adaptation on heterogeneous reasoning problems. There's a need for more adaptive strategies that account for instance difficulty and uncertainty.
AI.method: DiSCTT uses consensus among sampled reasoning trajectories to estimate epistemic uncertainty. High-consensus inputs undergo supervised fine-tuning using majority-agreed solutions as pseudo-labels. Low-consensus inputs are optimized via reinforcement learning with a consensus-regularized objective that encourages diversity under relevance constraints.
AI.result: Across mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks, DiSCTT consistently outperforms strong test-time adaptation baselines, achieving higher accuracy with reduced variance and substantially lower computation and wall-clock training times.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly accounting for instance difficulty and uncertainty enables more stable, efficient, and effective test-time adaptation for reasoning models, demonstrating the value of difficulty-aware, consensus-guided optimization strategies.

title: Progressive Residual Warmup for Language Model Pretraining
summary: Transformer architectures serve as the backbone for most modern Large Language Models, therefore their pretraining stability and convergence speed are of central concern. Motivated by the logical dependency of sequentially stacked layers, we propose Progressive Residual Warmup (ProRes) for language model pretraining. ProRes implements an "early layer learns first" philosophy by multiplying each layer's residual with a scalar that gradually warms up from 0 to 1, with deeper layers taking longer warmup steps. In this way, deeper layers wait for early layers to settle into a more stable regime before contributing to learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ProRes through pretraining experiments across various model scales, as well as normalization and initialization schemes. Comprehensive analysis shows that ProRes not only stabilizes pretraining but also introduces a unique optimization trajectory, leading to faster convergence, stronger generalization and better downstream performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/dandingsky/ProRes.

AI.tldr: Progressive Residual Warmup (ProRes) stabilizes transformer pretraining by gradually activating deeper layers, allowing early layers to stabilize first, leading to faster convergence and better performance.
AI.motivation: Transformer architectures are foundational for LLMs, but their pretraining stability and convergence speed remain challenging due to the logical dependency of sequentially stacked layers.
AI.method: ProRes multiplies each layer's residual with a scalar that gradually warms up from 0 to 1, with deeper layers taking longer warmup steps, implementing an "early layer learns first" philosophy.
AI.result: ProRes stabilizes pretraining, introduces a unique optimization trajectory, leads to faster convergence, stronger generalization, and better downstream performance across various model scales and configurations.
AI.conclusion: ProRes effectively addresses transformer pretraining stability by progressively activating deeper layers, offering a simple yet powerful technique for improving LLM training efficiency and performance.

title: An Exploration-Analysis-Disambiguation Reasoning Framework for Word Sense Disambiguation with Low-Parameter LLMs
summary: Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) remains a key challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP), especially when dealing with rare or domain-specific senses that are often misinterpreted.
